title: Parental responsibility: who has it, how it is acquired, care orders vs s20
blurb: Work out who holds parental responsibility for a child in front of you, and what changes under a care order or s20 accommodation.
question: Mason, 5, needs a planned general anaesthetic. He arrives with his father, who was never married to Mason's mother but is named on the birth certificate registered in 2021. The mother cannot be contacted. Can the father give consent?

teach.body: Parental responsibility (PR) is 'all the rights, duties, powers, responsibilities and authority which by law a parent of a child has in relation to the child and his property' (Children Act 1989 s3(1)). For nurses it answers a daily question: who can consent to treatment for a child who cannot consent for themselves? In plain English: PR is the legal right to make decisions for a child. Being a biological parent, a relative or the person who brought the child in does not by itself give PR.

children.label: Married or civil partner at birth?
children.sub: Yes: PR. No: see routes below

children.label: Not automatically
children.sub: Needs an order, agreement or guardianship

teach.caption: A second female parent under the HFEA 2008 can hold PR in the same way as a father.

teach.h: Routes to PR for an unmarried father (s4(1))
head: Route
Detail
rows: Named on the register: births registered from 1 Dec 2003 (England and Wales)
teach.caption: Re-registering the birth to add his name also gives PR when that registration is made on or after 1 Dec 2003, even for an older birth (Adoption and Children Act 2002 s111(7)).
A step-parent gains PR by a s4A agreement with each parent who holds PR, or by a court order. A person named in a child arrangements order as someone the child lives with also has PR.

teach.h: PR is shared, delegated, not transferred
teach.body: Several people can hold PR at once. PR cannot be surrendered or transferred, but a holder can arrange for some of it to be met by someone acting on their behalf, such as a grandparent doing the school run (s2(9)). A person who has care of a child without PR may do what is reasonable to safeguard or promote the child's welfare (s3(5)): for example, bringing the child to hospital and giving a history. Major or elective decisions need someone with PR, or the competent child.

rows.label: Parents' PR
values: Kept, but shared with the LA

rows.label: Removal
values: Any PR holder at any time

teach.caption: s20(7)-(8): the LA cannot accommodate if a PR holder able to care objects, and any PR holder may remove the child. s20(11): not if a 16 or 17-year-old agrees to accommodation.

teach.body: Mason's parents were not married, so his father does not have PR by marriage. But he is on the birth register for a 2021 birth in England, so under s4(1)(a) he acquired PR on registration. He can consent to the anaesthetic. The nurse confirms identity and records how PR was established, as local policy requires. If he were not on the certificate, he would need a PR agreement or court order, and the team would contact the mother.

teach.text: Looked after does not always mean the local authority has PR. Under a care order the LA shares PR with the parents; under s20 accommodation it has none, and parents keep full PR and may remove the child. Check which applies before accepting a social worker's consent.

steps.label: Record
steps.sub: Who consented and on what basis

items: Mother: always PR. Father: PR if married to (or civil partner of) the mother at birth.
Unmarried father: birth registration (births registered from 1 Dec 2003, England and Wales), PR agreement or court order.
Step-parents and grandparents: no PR without an agreement, order or guardianship.
Care order: LA shares PR with parents. s20 accommodation: LA has no PR; parents can remove the child.
PR can be delegated but not transferred (s2(9)); carers without PR may do what is reasonable (s3(5)).

summary: You can now identify who holds parental responsibility, including unmarried fathers, step-parents and second female parents. You can also explain how a care order and s20 accommodation differ in who can consent and who can remove the child.

A.q: Isla, 8, attends day surgery with her grandmother, who has cared for her every weekday for three years. Isla's mother holds PR and has not delegated anything in writing. What does the grandmother's position give her?
options: PR by virtue of providing regular day-to-day care
PR because she is a close relative under the Act
Authority to do what is reasonable, but no PR
Full PR once Isla has lived with her for three years
A.why: Grandparents do not have PR automatically. Under s3(5) a person with care of a child may do what is reasonable to safeguard or promote welfare, but elective surgery needs consent from a PR holder.

whyNot.0: Regular care does not create PR.
whyNot.1: Being a relative does not create PR.
whyNot.3: There is no time-based route to PR from caring alone.

A.q: Which of these fathers holds parental responsibility for his child?
options: Unmarried, and the birth registered in 2001 without his name
Unmarried, and named on the register of a 2019 birth
Divorced from the mother before the child was conceived
Unmarried, and paying child maintenance by court order
A.why: s4(1)(a): an unmarried father who is registered as the father acquires PR, for births registered in England and Wales from 1 December 2003.

whyNot.0: Not named, and in any case before the registration route began.
whyNot.2: Divorced before conception means not married at the birth, so no PR by marriage.
whyNot.3: A maintenance order does not confer PR.

A.q: Bea, 10, is accommodated under section 20 with her mother's agreement while her mother is in hospital. Who can consent to Bea's planned grommet surgery?
options: Her mother, who keeps parental responsibility
The local authority, which holds PR while she is accommodated
The foster carer, who acquires PR on placement
The independent reviewing officer for the placement
A.why: s20 accommodation does not give the local authority PR; Bea's mother keeps it and is the person to consent.

whyNot.1: The local authority gains PR under a care order, not under s20.
whyNot.2: Foster carers do not acquire PR by placement.
whyNot.3: The reviewing officer has no PR.

B.q: Kai, 6, lives with his mother and stepfather, who married four years ago. There is no agreement or court order about the stepfather. He brings Kai for an elective tonsillectomy. What is the best action?
options: Accept his consent, as he has lived with Kai for over two years
Accept his consent, as marriage to a PR holder confers PR
Accept his consent, because Kai's mother told him to attend
Contact the mother, as the stepfather does not have PR
B.why: Marriage to a parent does not give a step-parent PR: it needs a s4A agreement or order, or another order such as a child arrangements order. Elective consent should come from a PR holder, so the team contacts Kai's mother.

whyNot.0: Living together does not create PR.
whyNot.1: Marrying a PR holder does not by itself confer PR on a step-parent.
whyNot.2: Arranging for him to attend is not consent from a PR holder to surgery.

B.q: Remi, 9, is subject to a care order and lives with foster carers. His birth father, who has PR, asks the nurse whether he has lost it. What is accurate?
options: Yes, a care order transfers PR to the local authority
No, he keeps PR, shared with the local authority
Yes, but he regains it once Remi turns 16
No, and the local authority has no PR in that case
B.why: Under a care order the local authority acquires PR and shares it with parents, who keep theirs.

whyNot.0: PR cannot be transferred; a care order adds the LA as a holder.
whyNot.2: He has not lost PR, so there is nothing to regain.
whyNot.3: The LA does acquire PR under a care order.

B.q: A child accommodated under s20 is visited on the ward by her father, who has PR and a suitable home. He says he is taking her home today. What does the law allow?
options: He needs written agreement from the social worker first
He must give 28 days' notice to the local authority
He may remove her, as any PR holder can end s20 accommodation
He may remove her once a court formally discharges the arrangement
B.why: s20(8): any person with PR may at any time remove the child from s20 accommodation. If there are safety concerns, the nurse informs social care and the safeguarding team at once.

whyNot.0: No social worker agreement is required under s20(8).
whyNot.1: There is no notice period in s20.
whyNot.3: s20 is voluntary; no court is involved in ending it.

C.q: Zara, 16, has been staying in s20 accommodation at her own request after arguments at home. Her mother, who has PR, objects and wants her home. What is the legal position?
options: Zara can stay, as her agreement at 16 overrides it
Zara must go home, as a PR holder can remove her at any time
Zara can stay until a court decides between them
Zara must go home unless a care order is made
C.why: s20(11): the parental objection and removal rights in s20(7)-(8) do not apply where a child aged 16 or over agrees to be accommodated.

whyNot.1: The removal right does not apply when a 16 or 17-year-old agrees to accommodation.
whyNot.2: No court decision is needed; s20(11) settles it.
whyNot.3: A care order is not needed for Zara to remain accommodated with her agreement.

C.q: Two women were civil partners when their son Leo, 3, was conceived by licensed fertility treatment. The non-birth mother attends alone for his planned dental extractions under anaesthesia. What should the nurse conclude?
options: She needs a parental order before she can consent
She can consent, as a legal parent with PR
She needs the birth mother's written delegation
She can consent once she adopts Leo formally
C.why: A second female parent who was the civil partner of the birth mother at the time of treatment is a legal parent with PR (HFEA 2008), in the same way as a married father.

whyNot.0: A parental order applies to surrogacy, not this situation.
whyNot.2: She holds PR herself, so delegation is not needed.
whyNot.3: Adoption is not needed; she is already a legal parent.

C.q: A father who was never married to the mother brings Ana, 4, for planned surgery. Ana's birth was registered in 2022 with only the mother's name; he was added on re-registration last year. A colleague says he cannot consent. Which response is correct?
options: He cannot, as PR comes from the original registration
He cannot, as he must also have a PR agreement
He can, if the mother confirms by telephone first
He can, as re-registration naming him gives PR
C.why: Becoming registered as the father, including by re-registration, is a s4(1)(a) route to PR for births registered in England and Wales from 1 December 2003.

whyNot.0: Re-registration is a recognised route; it need not be the original entry.
whyNot.1: Registration is an alternative to an agreement, not an extra step.
whyNot.2: He holds PR in his own right, so the mother's confirmation is not required.

reteach.title: Who signs for the child?
reteach.question: How can I quickly work out who holds parental responsibility?

blocks.body: Ask three questions. Is this the birth mother? She always has PR. Is this a father or second parent who was married to, or the civil partner of, the mother at the birth? Then PR. If not, has PR been added since: by the birth register, an agreement, a court order, adoption or special guardianship? Anyone else, however close, needs one of those routes. Then check for orders: a care order adds the local authority as a PR holder; s20 does not.

blocks.text: Care order = LA shares PR. s20 = LA has no PR. Grandparents and step-parents have none by default.

explain.body: The birth mother always has PR. A father, or a second female parent, has PR if married to or in a civil partnership with the mother at the time of the birth.

test.q: Which person has PR without any registration, agreement or order?
options: A maternal grandmother who is the child's main carer
An unmarried father who lives with the child
A father married to the mother when the child was born
A stepmother who has been married to the child's father for years
test.why: Marriage to the mother at the time of birth gives a father PR automatically (s2(1)).

whyNot.0: Grandparents need an order or guardianship.
whyNot.1: Living together does not give an unmarried father PR.
whyNot.3: A stepmother needs a s4A agreement or order.

explain.body: Three routes in s4(1): registration as the father (births registered from 1 December 2003 in England and Wales), a PR agreement with the mother, or a court order.

test.q: An unmarried father of a child born in 2000 is not on the birth certificate. How can he gain PR now?
options: By showing a DNA test that proves paternity
By paying child maintenance for the past year
By living with the child as his father for at least a year
By a PR agreement with the mother or a court order
test.why: He can gain PR through a PR agreement with the mother or a court order (s4(1)(b)-(c)); if the birth is later re-registered with his name, that also gives PR.

whyNot.0: Proof of paternity does not itself confer PR.
whyNot.1: Maintenance payments do not confer PR.
whyNot.2: Living with the child does not confer PR.

explain.body: PR cannot be transferred, but holders can arrange for others to act for them (s2(9)). Someone with care but no PR may do what is reasonable to safeguard the child's welfare (s3(5)).

test.q: A childminder brings a 3-year-old to the ED after a fall. Neither parent can yet be reached. What does s3(5) allow her to do?
options: Take what reasonable steps the child's welfare needs
Consent to elective surgery on the parents' behalf
Transfer the parents' PR to the hospital temporarily
Refuse any treatment that she believes is unnecessary for the child
test.why: s3(5) lets a person with care of a child do what is reasonable in all the circumstances to safeguard or promote the child's welfare, such as bringing the child in and giving a history.

whyNot.1: Elective decisions need a PR holder.
whyNot.3: Refusing needed treatment is not a reasonable step for welfare.

explain.body: A care order (court) gives the local authority PR, shared with parents. s20 accommodation (agreement) gives the LA no PR; parents keep it and can remove the child, unless a child of 16 or 17 agrees to stay.

test.q: A social worker asks to sign consent for a child accommodated under s20. What should the nurse do?
options: Accept it, as the LA holds PR under s20
Accept it if the child's foster carer agrees
Seek consent from a parent who holds PR
Seek consent from the independent reviewing officer
test.why: Under s20 the local authority has no PR; consent comes from a parent with PR (or the competent child).

whyNot.0: The LA acquires PR under a care order, not s20.
whyNot.1: Foster carers do not hold PR.
whyNot.3: The reviewing officer has no PR.
